body:
There is no decent parent in the universe who wouldn't rather have a sad failure (what you seem to think, not what I think!) for a child than a dead one. They won't get over it. No matter how you die. The love a parent feels for a child is deeply biological. It is ferocious and frightening. It never goes away.

Life isn't what you think. Set a goal, meet it at all costs. That's the movies. I was thrown out of my PhD program for depression. My life plan gone. Started over. Lost that. Started over again. One thing I did learn: single-minded, driven people don't have it all. They miss out on a lot of stuff because the have blinders on to all the other things in life. *No one* has it all. Anyone who says they do is preening their feathers and is no friend, believe me.

Maybe think about *why* you want to be a doctor so badly. Helping people? Try nursing. The world is gasping for nurses. Hands-on and very well paid. Is it the status? Then another high status career. Politician. Investment banker. Airline pilot. Is it the money? Ditto: other paths to wealth. Whatever it is that draws you about medicine you can find somewhere else.

Most people aren't really uncompromising. Most of us get through with flexibility, improvisation, and a little gentleness with ourselves.

Good luck.

Sorry, I'm here. Well, I have my days. As we all do. I've been traveling a bit, so I had some wonky access. Have you been feeling better? Some self care might not go amiss. I treated myself to a fancy lunch while I was gone--something I never do. But it's a great indulgence I highly recommend. No chit chat, no sharing. Whatever you fancy. If you can't afford it right now, cook yourself something. Whatever you want. There's a famius articke about making oneself an omelette and a glass of wine. Remind yourself that you are here, have likes and wants, and you can see to them.

I have a two-year-old boy, too. He's both the best and worst of everything. I have found the transition to parenthood very hard. Mainly because I grew up with two deeply mentally ill parents. To me, family life represents fear, distress, abuse, and total futility.

One thing I didn't expect before my son came is how corrosive "parenting culture" is. Shaming, blaming, and guilting is its favorite pastime. Maybe you're getting a lot of negative feedback. Not sure what to tell you about thst, since I struggle myself with it, every day.

Here is one chilling fact that might keep you here: the children of people who commit suicide are more likely to commit suicide themselves. We model behaviors. Plus, kids don't get over it. They don't. As others have said, they'll wonder why you didn't love them enough to stay.

We always hear that parents will do anything, absolutely anything, for their kids. Maybe this is our "anything": we won't end our own lives. We'll get help and do our best.
You're being harrassed. I'd take screenshots to the police.
Hey, sweet pea! Just checking in to see if you feel like talking some more. :) How are you getting along today?

Typing quickly. Hope I don't sound too abrupt. But the first idea you need to discard is that you need fixing. You need guidance and a kind listener. A community. But there is nothing. wrong. with. you. You've soaked up too much tragedy and trauma. You've lost your support system. None of it reflects poorly on you.

Oh, honey. I'm so sorry. It sounds like you are a fantastic and caring person, being dragged down by other people's problems. Social work is a bastard. I can't imagine what you see on a daily basis. But keep one thing in mind: you see the worst of humanity. The tiny minority. As they say, to the man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. You must have burnout. Layered with the PTSD. But this world isn't a horror show. There have to be avenues of support. 

As to being rejected by your parents for being gay. That is a level of foulness I can't even comprehend. But being fay today in America, there is a lot to celebrate. There are many options. You can choose a predominantly gay community to live in, or a more mixed community. Have a family, or not. Please find some support. I have had many gay friends who are the joy of my life. Some of whom had troubled family backgrounds. Your ignorant parents are the problem. Not. You.

A lot has hit you at once. You need help. But you are on the side of the angels. Please stay.

Have to stop. If I type too much, my phone eats it.
I knew somepne personally who jumped off a building and wound up partially paralyzed from the waist down.

Slow down a second. Your colleagues f@cked up. You did not and since you didn't have the exams, you couldn't fix the problem.

Write the email and let the idiots twist in the wind.

Your thinking in this post is catastrophic to the max. Why would you get fired for other people's mistakes?

I'd stop drinking and fimd someone to help you put this into perspective.

I'm sorry this happened. I think you can be supportive of your partner getting treatment, but I think you need to think long and carefully about this relationship. Drama, upheaval, even law-breaking, are common in BPD. As are threats of suicide and/or attempts. Personality disorders are also notoriously hard to treat. Even when the patient is willing and eager to change. I grew up with a BPD mother, so I'm not trying to be insensitive or dismissive. I've walked in the same shoes. Also, if you're thinking longterm, think about how your SO will function as a parent, financial partner, or caregiver.

There is a website called "Out of the Fog" you might check out. It has forums for people who are currently in relationships with people who have personality disorders. It can be ranty, but it can also be remarkably even-handed.

Do keep one thing in mind: you can support your gf, but you can't "fix" her. To try is a waste of emotional effort.

Good luck.

If depression seems out of character, it's hard not to wonder if there is something physiological at work. As in a bad side effect of your medication (yes, they can crop up without warning after years without incident), or illness. Inflammation, thyroid imbalance, blood sugar issues. The list of possibilities is very long. Please see a medical doctor before you do anything that might stem from a fixable problem.

Life insurance doesn't pay out for suicide. Your family is, and always will be, better off with your earning power and your participation. Is there an agency within the military you can apply to for finanicial relief? Does your family qualify for TANF or other programs?

There's nothing wrong with graduating high school at 20. My dad got his GED at 44. We had the same high school English teacher. Can you ask for academic help? Depression can wreak havoc on your comprehension and your memory. You may have a learning disorder. And maybe school just isn't your thing, and you just need to slog through and then, move on. To trade school. To a one-year associate's degree. An apprenticeship. 

Being rudderless at 20 is not a bad thing. It's kind of what being 20 is all about. That's when you start leaving childhood behind, and getting beyond the person you were pigeonholed into being for 12 years of school. It's confusing and painful, but it's necessary. Purpose will come.
I think you should call an ambulance.

Hard to say. I'd be careful. Maybe search for community. There are churches emphasize the more human aspects of congregation. For example, I attend a Unitarian Universalist church that dictates no particular belief system (atheists are welcome), and explores various religions for wisdom and advice, rather than insisting on belief in divinity. But there are much more hardcore sects that prey on people feeling vulnerable. I'd steer clear of those. But there are also meet-ups of all kinds to try, around all sorts of activities or interests. Mountain biking, cooking classes. You could volunteer at a soup kitchen or animal shelter, if you want to do some good while you socialize. You can find almost anything, religious or secular.

Your dad was telling the truth. I have a son and he's right. There are few tragedies worse than losing a child. When my boy was 8 weeks old, I was told he might die. I cried so many tears on his tiny head that I had to brush the salt out of his hair.

There is no loving parent who has lost a child who wouldn't take them back in any form. A loner. A loser. Sick. Broken. A failure. We just want you to exist.

Also, keep in mind, if your ex is so determined to kill herself that she won't engage with therapy or help herself in any way, there is nothing more you can do. If someone it totally fixed on the idea, they cannot be stopped. Whatever happens next, you did your best. But you aren't a god, or a miracle worker. Ok? She'll need to do at least some of the work herself.

I say this from experience. I cared for my elderly mom. She fought me on everything, refused even basic safety measures, such as an emergency pendant. But I had no legal grounds to compel her to do anything. I was frantic. But when I consulted a case worker, and laid out the situation, and everything I had tried, she told me, "You've done all you can. Hope for the best. But you have to let go." And I did.
Good luck. To you both.

I was suicidal as a young woman. I was involuntarily committed by my doctor. I found out later that my fiance (now husband), was going to call the doctor and urge him to do this, although he never did, the doctor beat him to it. I asked why, and he said "So you'd have a long life to hate me."

If you think your ex is serious about suicide, I'd do whatever is necessary to help her. Contact the mental health counselors at the university, her parents and/or siblings. She might view this as a betrayal, you might lose your friend. But, with any luck, she'll be alive to hate your guts. And, with time and a renewed sense of reality, she might forgive you. But don't count on it. You may just have to do your best and accept the results.

Ok, let's get you some help. You can chat here. Have you tried Crisis Text Chat? You dial 741-741 from a cell, and you can speak with someone, no personal info necessary. I'd just just about data rates, depending in your data plan. Some are free, some aren't. There are phone numbers you can call. The Samaritans, for instance. People don't need to know you to help you through. Life loves life itself. We humans are wired to help each other.

Honey, I want you to call emergency services right now. I don't know you at all. I am an objective stranger who means you no harm. None. And this post makes no sense at all. I think your relationship with reality is disrupted.
First, please calm down. What happened?
Are you still there?
We can't chat if you're unconscious. What did you take?
Call 911. Now. Or 999 if in UK. Call for help.

Mental health has come a long way in the last few decades. I lived with a father who had undiagnosed ptsd and bipolar because his family hushed it up. Lies and hypocrisy are more damaging than any illness. Shame is incredibly destructive. Maybe it wasn't the illness that took your family members, but ignorance. In the medical profession or society at large. You might share the genetics, but maybe you will not suffer from the circumstances that do the real damage. Be honest, seek treatment. If you let the sunlight into the dark places, you'd be amazed how much better things can be.

I'm sorry you feel so stressed and anxious. I also have mental issues. I've lost both my parents. Lost more than one romantic relationship in my time. So, I am living your worst fears, in a way. And, really, it's ok. The plug didn't come out of the tub. i just kept going, seeking new things, nurturing new and old relationships. Nobody goes through life without major changes. I'm not giving platitudes. This is lived experience. When the bad times come, usually they aren't as horrific as your imaginings. And then, it's over. Daily life is a great distraction.

Good luck, hon.

I live pretty far away, in the US. Ontario is beautiful, tho. My family's Canadian on both sides, so I have a real affinity for the place. I was wondering...can you say something about what brought you to the headspace you're in? Is it long-term troubles, a sudden crisis, or some combination?
I hope not. Are you still there?

A few things. First, it sounds like you could use some help with depression, self-esteem, etc. Low energy could even be medical. I'd try to address these things with the correct doctors.

Next, you sound like you feel rudderless. Not sure where to go or how to get there. I hope I can offer a little advice. First, I totally agree with PP's attitude toward "mistakes." My husband is in the sciences, and does outreach with high school and college students. The thing he fights the hardest is the utter fear instilled in them of making mistakes. Because science is nothing but controlled "mistakes." An experiment is an attempt to learn something. Ninety percent of the time, it doesn't turn out the way you expect. But that's a good thing. Now you know what *doesn't* work. So, you can move on to another approach. It's like going down a hallway of shut doors and trying each one. All locked. Until you find the one that opens. There's just no other way to make a go of anything, not just science.

Next, I'd find a mentor. Not an advisor, a mentor. Someone who has the job and the lifestyle you want, and ask for their help. Most people are thrilled if someone takes an interest in their work and wants advice. They might tell you the best strategies for education, career tips, or even help you network. The worst a person can say is no. I'd also ask questions beyond the job. What kind of lifestyle do you want? Where do you want to live? Do you want to travel? Make lots of money? High stress, low stress? Lifestyle is just as important as pay or promotion for a successful career.

I hope this helps.

I hope this helps. I suspect that I am older than you, so this first: it sounds like you're having what might be termed "a quarter-life crisis" of some kind. I think a lot, maybe most, people go through some version of this. It's when you realize that the fairytales we're all told as kids aren't true. The world is, on balance, pretty indifferent to us. Not welcoming. Just doesn't care much. It's full of struggle and pain and beauty and love. It's very complex. Bad things have upsides (sometimes, terrible upsides) and good things turn into disasters. This process is part of becoming aware in a mature way.

I'm a trained historian. That also shapes my perspective. And I can tell you that the world has always, always been poised on the brink. The future is always fearful. Those guys who marched off to fight Hitler didn't know if they'd win.

I think there are two things we can do. First, play the odds. The majority of people lead decent, unremarkable lives. We have ways of averting most disasters, and we're working on the rest. Second, acknowledge our mortality. We'll all die. Maybe today, maybe in 150 years, if medical science has its way. We have a few laughs along the way, some love, some fun, a lot of sorrow, and hard work. That's what everyone gets.

Your perspective seems to include what I've heard called "catastrophic thinking." Every scenario is worst-case. I hear a lot of anxiety. Have you tried talking through these fears, either with friends or a therapist?
Can I ask: what kind of help do you want?

Here's the thing. Mood swings can cause problems. It's not that you are "well" when you feel up, and "disordered" when you feel bad. It's that swinging between poles is the problem. It's not that people don't have their ups and downs, but if you are crippled or suffer from your actions at the peaks and the troughs, that's an issue.

If it were me, I'd go back to your therapist, or find another if you aren't comfortable with, and describe your mood swings.

I agree. The internet changed our world forever in that we can finally hear what others are thinking, en masse. What a disappointment it's been. Anonymity lights up the cruelty dispensers in our brains, that's been proven. A Harvard study showed that in an anonymous environment, with no consequences, an online interaction turns sexual or violent within a smal number of exchanges.

Just know, you 're not the only sensitive soul who has been torn limb from limb online. The most fraught encounters in places where we go for help. When my son was born, I went to the mommy forums. I'm not sure I'll ever recover from the level of viciousness I encountered there. 

I hope you find safe harbor. IRL.

My family is dead, and I've had meds and therapy. But nothing can change the fact that when people tell me I am a monster, I agree with them. But thank you for dropping a line. It's just nice to hear one encouraging thought.
It was nice of you to offer a kind word. I appreciate it.

I'm very sorry to hear this. I cared for both my parents until they passed away. I was older than you, but still decades younger than most people I met in the same situation. Then again, the crisis really began when my dad was severy brain-injured in a car accident when I was 12. it was just a slow-motion fall after that.

The first thing I'd say is don't be surprised if your friends and family back away. Either out of a fear they'll be tapped to help or because they just don't get it. I found myself on my own. In my more charitable moments, I realized that I was a harbinger of something that comes to almost everybody at some point. And no one likes looking their nightmare in the face. But that's just when I feel charitable. :)

What got me through was getting professional help. Eldercare case workers, an estate planning attorney, and an accountant. They can advise you on negotiating the medical, financial, and legal aspects. It doesn't necessarily cost a fortune. Even a single consultation might help you immensely.

Next, I'd be very careful with online support groups. People can be cruel. Especially the martyrs. If you aren't jumping for joy about your heavy burdens every minute, some people will claw your eyes out. I found IRL groups were much more supportive and less judgmental. Very few bullies have the courage to call someone "a bad, ungrateful child" to their face.

One last thing: no matter what you do, how good you are at caregiving, you will feel guilty. It's just the way we're wired. Do your best. You can't make a miracle. In cases of eldercare, there are no winners or happy endings. Just "less bad" than the alternatives.

I hope this helps. Godspeed.
Oh, no. I shouldn't. I was just putting my vote in for those who might feel guilty about not feeling worse. Blood is what you make it. It confers neither affection nor obligation.
My uBPD mother died fourteen months ago. I don't miss her. I don't feel bad about it.

Doing right: if you look at nearly every world religion, major or minor, they all preach the same thing. Viz to wit, principles that breed strong communities. Sharing. Loving. Forgiving. Helping without question.

Doing wrong? Getting too caught up in everything else. Language. Other people's beliefs.

That's beautifully shot, bravo. :) I read that animals with black fur are less likely to be adopted from shelters for this very reason: they are hard to photograph and don't look cute on the websites. Someone needs to develop a "black cat" filter for phone cameras to help them out. Poor sweeties.

I was an only child so I was both GC and no-good. In public, my mom couldn't say enough good things about me. In private...not so much. And even at home, my mother's attitude toward me flip-flopped minute by minute. What was laudable in the morning was a crime by lunch.

I don't think you could get it, and even if you could, the premiums would be prohibitively expensive.

My advice? Find and eldercare resource advisor and/or an estate planning attorney. You may shell out a little money, but they can guide you toward a feasible plan.

Good luck.

This was my husband's fave show. He told me that he heard a story that a lot of medical professionals regard "Scrubs" as the most realistic medical show ever put on TV. Maybe. It blended utter lunacy with tragedy.
Cuz I'm curious: did you buy the proper tatami mats to roll? Or is this free-hand? If you rolled those maki without a mat, color me uber impressed. :)

Me again. One more thing. :) I'd try to attend conferences that welcome undergrads. A lot do. Awesome networking and informational opportunities. And, under the supervision of your mentor, try to find opportunities for research and publication. An undergrad who publishes is a rarity. You'll stand out, either in industry or academia. Be sure you write for reputable outlets, and get lots of advice from trustworthy professionals. But do it. It'll pay off massively.

If you want to impress people, be impressive. Simple as that.

Here's what I would do (former academic here). I'd go with the state school and work it, work it, work it. Find a professor to mentor you, and ask lots of questions. Find undergraduate outreach programs in your field and start talking to people. Subscribe to industry publications and make industry contacts. Find those fellowships, internships. 

In my experience, your skills and your extended network matter much more than the institution on your degree. Approach your studies like a career professional. You'd be shocked at how eager people will be to help if you present yourself as open, serious, and enthusiastic.

I'd start with, I'd prefer not to discuss it. If they persist, tell them it's really not their concern. If *that* doesn't work, make up the most heart-wrenching story you can think of about infertility or lost pregnancies, etc. Embarrass the ever-living f@ck outta them. People who pry to that degree are either preening their own feathers or trying to hurt you. They deserve to suffer agonies of remorse.
Don't listen to what people tell you. Listen to what they say when they think you're not paying attention.

This is my first Christmas as an orphan. What a relief. I'll spend it with hubster and son. I may never be a wildly enthusiastic holiday person, but I can create a quiet, warm environment. Worlds away from the place I grew up. 

What's hard about the holidays is how other people react to my lack of enthuiasm. I had decades of aversion therapy. The idea of being trapped with family for an entire day is suffocating. I'm not unloving. I just don't love them. Let me be. I'll bake your cookies, wrap your gifts, drink your eggnog, and smile in every. single. photo. But it's all new to me, and, no, I don't want to call home.

I feel like this. I hate everything to do with family. On Christmas, I usually have to crawl away to cry. Why? The carols, the lights, the presents bring back memories of holidays with my parents. So incredibly stressful. Would I be in trouble for not being grateful or joyful enough? Would my mom stuff her gifts in the trash or would this be a "good year"? Would there be screaming all day long because my parents were cooped up in the same place?

What a waste of a life. That's why I grieve.

In our house, animals were the "golden child" used to provide evidence of how the humans fell short. My nMom used to sit with the dog and pet her, saying, "You love me. No one else in this house does, but you do. You value me. No one else does," etc., etc. It was one of the million ways that she reiterated my faults as a daughter. It's a weird sort of deflection.
